## Unintentional close calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Unintentional close calls")]

Unintentional use close calls may occur due to equipment failure. Common examples are strategic bombers accidentally dropping or crashing with nuclear bombs, or [early warning systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_warning_systems "Early warning systems") mistaking phenomena such as [weather events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_events_during_wars "Weather events during wars") or non-nuclear rocket launches for an [ICBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ICBM "ICBM")[first strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_strike_(nuclear_strategy) "First strike (nuclear strategy)") and therefore recommending a [second strike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_strike "Second strike").

### 1957: U.S. accidental bomb drop in New Mexico

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: 1957: U.S. accidental bomb drop in New Mexico")]

A [B-36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-36 "B-36") accidentally dropped a bomb just south of [Albuquerque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albuquerque "Albuquerque"), [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"). Due to safety measures, the plutonium core was not mounted to the bomb at the time but rather stored elsewhere in the plane, preventing a [nuclear detonation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_explosion "Nuclear explosion"). The conventional explosives created a 7.6 m (25 ft)-wide crater on impact.

### 1958: U.S. accidental bomb drop in Savannah, Georgia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: 1958: U.S. accidental bomb drop in Savannah, Georgia")]

A bomb was mistakenly dropped by a [U.S. Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Air_Force "U.S. Air Force")[Boeing B-47E-LM Stratojet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_B-47E-LM_Stratojet "Boeing B-47E-LM Stratojet") near [Savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savannah,_Georgia "Savannah, Georgia"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), when a man in the [bomb bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bomb_bay "Bomb bay") area grabbed the emergency release pin by accident. Similar to the 1957 incident, safety precautions meant that the plutonium was not mounted to the bomb but rather stored elsewhere on the plane at the time.

### 1960: U.S. false alarm from moonrise

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: 1960: U.S. false alarm from moonrise")]

Radar equipment in [Thule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thule_Air_Base "Thule Air Base"), [Greenland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"), mistakenly interpreted a [moonrise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonrise_and_moonset "Moonrise and moonset") over [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway") as a large-scale [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") missile launch. Upon receiving a report of the supposed attack, [NORAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NORAD "NORAD") went on high alert. However, doubts about the authenticity of the attack arose due to the presence of Soviet leader [Nikita Khrushchev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Khrushchev "Nikita Khrushchev") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") as head of the USSR's [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") delegation.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-UCS_close_calls-87)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-K_Blows_Top-88)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-89)

### 1961: U.S. strategic bomber crash in North Carolina

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: 1961: U.S. strategic bomber crash in North Carolina")]

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Goldsboro_Bomb_Weapon_1_%28LA-UR-20-22180%29.jpg/250px-Goldsboro_Bomb_Weapon_1_%28LA-UR-20-22180%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Goldsboro_Bomb_Weapon_1_(LA-UR-20-22180).jpg)

One of Mark 39 nuclear bombs after the 1961 incident near Goldsboro, North Carolina

A [B-52 Stratofortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-52_Stratofortress "B-52 Stratofortress") carrying two 3–4-[megaton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNT_equivalent#Kiloton_and_megaton "TNT equivalent")[Mark 39 nuclear bombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_39_nuclear_bomb "Mark 39 nuclear bomb") broke up in mid-air near [Goldsboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldsboro,_North_Carolina "Goldsboro, North Carolina"), [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), dropping its nuclear payload in the process.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-90) The pilot in command, Walter Scott Tulloch, ordered the crew to [eject](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejection_seat "Ejection seat") at 9,000 feet (2,700 m). Five crewmen successfully ejected or bailed out of the aircraft and landed safely, another ejected but did not survive the landing, and two died in the crash.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-91)

Information declassified in 2013 showed that "only a single switch prevented the ... bomb from detonating and spreading fire and destruction over a wide area."[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-92) An expert evaluation written on 22 October 1969 by Parker F. Jones, the supervisor of the nuclear weapons safety department at [Sandia National Laboratories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandia_National_Laboratories "Sandia National Laboratories"), reported that "one simple, [dynamo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamo "Dynamo")-technology, low voltage switch stood between the United States and a major catastrophe", and that it "seems credible" that a short circuit in the Arm line during a mid-air breakup of the aircraft "could" have resulted in a nuclear explosion.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-guardian-goldsboro-revisted-93)

### 1961: U.S. strategic bomber crash in California

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: 1961: U.S. strategic bomber crash in California")]

A [B-52 Stratofortress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-52_Stratofortress "B-52 Stratofortress") carrying two nuclear weapons experienced a catastrophic [decompression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncontrolled_decompression "Uncontrolled decompression"), eventually forcing the crew to eject. The crewless plane crashed 15 miles west of [Yuba City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuba_City "Yuba City"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). The bombs did not detonate due to safety features.

### 1961: U.S. false alarm from communications failure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: 1961: U.S. false alarm from communications failure")]

Staff at the [Strategic Air Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command "Strategic Air Command") Headquarters (SAC HQ) simultaneously lost contact with NORAD and multiple [Ballistic Missile Early Warning System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistic_Missile_Early_Warning_System "Ballistic Missile Early Warning System") sites. Since these communication lines were designed to be redundant and independent from one another, the communications failure was interpreted as either a very unlikely coincidence or a coordinated attack. SAC HQ prepared the entire ready force for takeoff before already overhead aircraft confirmed that there did not appear to be an attack. It was later found that the failure of a single relay station in [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado") was the sole cause of the communications problem.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-UCS_close_calls-87)

### 1962: U.S. mistaken order during Cuban Missile Crisis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: 1962: U.S. mistaken order during Cuban Missile Crisis")]

According to a technician who served there, a mistaken order was issued by [Kadena Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadena_Air_Base "Kadena Air Base") in [Okinawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okinawa_Prefecture "Okinawa Prefecture") to nuclear missile sites in Okinawa to launch all their nuclear missiles. None were launched. A team responsible for four missiles at [Bolo Airfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolo_Airfield "Bolo Airfield") in [Yomitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yomitan "Yomitan") reported that the order's codes were in order, but the local officer in charge did not trust the order, partly because only one of their four missiles was targeted on Russia, and he saw no logic why missiles would be launched against China too, and because readiness was at [DEFCON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DEFCON "DEFCON") 2, not DEFCON 1.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-apj-94) Others serving there at the time have made statements saying they doubt this incident ever happened.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-95)

### 1964: U.S. strategic bomber crash in Maryland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: 1964: U.S. strategic bomber crash in Maryland")]

A B-52 carrying nuclear bombs was severely damaged while flying in turbulence over Western [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"). The plane crashed in [Garrett County, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrett_County,_Maryland "Garrett County, Maryland"), at [Savage River State Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savage_River_State_Forest "Savage River State Forest"). Having completed an [Operation Chrome Dome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Chrome_Dome "Operation Chrome Dome") mission, the plane was traveling from [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts") to [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)") carrying two nuclear bombs. Reports on the condition of the bombs varied, with [Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") (DoD) saying they were "relatively intact" while [Sandia National Laboratories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandia_National_Laboratories "Sandia National Laboratories") engineers saying they "broke apart" and that it was too risky to hastily move them. Within two days, the bombs were retrieved and taken to a local airport for transportation to Air Force facilities. The pilot ordered the crew to eject from the plane when it lost control. Three crew members died in the crash or due to exposure in the snowy winter conditions.

### 1965: U.K. false alarm due to misunderstood test plan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: 1965: U.K. false alarm due to misunderstood test plan")]

In 1965, Flight Lieutenant Tony Dobbie was serving as a duty officer at the Bomber Command Operations Centre (BCOC) at RAF High Wycombe following the disbandment of No. 15 Squadron.

During a shift, BCOC received notification that the Ballistic Missile Early Warning System (BMEWS) station at RAF Fylingdales was scheduled to run a system test. Fylingdales requested that the BCOC wall display remain set to "AUTOMATIC" rather than "TEST" while running the test tape. Because automatic mode caused test data to render as genuine threat alerts, the BCOC display registered an incoming missile strike marked as "REAL."

Unaware that the display reflected a test run, the duty controller instructed Dobbie to issue "Alert State 02" without an exercise code prefix. This order brought the Royal Air Force Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) V-bomber force to runway readiness. Upon detecting the unauthorized alert broadcast, staff at RAF Fylingdales disconnected the test tape and notified BCOC, allowing a stand-down order to be issued before aircraft were launched.

### 1965: U.S. false alarm from blackout computer errors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: 1965: U.S. false alarm from blackout computer errors")]

The Command Center of the [Office of Emergency Planning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives_Office_of_Emergency_Planning,_Preparedness,_and_Operations "United States House of Representatives Office of Emergency Planning, Preparedness, and Operations") went on full alert after a [massive power outage in the northeastern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_blackout_of_1965 "Northeast blackout of 1965"). Several nuclear bomb detectors—used to distinguish between regular power outages and power outages caused by a nuclear blast—near major U.S. cities malfunctioned due to circuit errors, creating the illusion of a [nuclear attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_warfare "Nuclear warfare").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-nuclear_files_20-5)

### 1965: U.S. attack aircraft falling off carrier

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: 1965: U.S. attack aircraft falling off carrier")]

During a training exercise in the [Philippine Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Sea "Philippine Sea"), a nuclear-armed [Douglas A-4 Skyhawk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_A-4_Skyhawk "Douglas A-4 Skyhawk") attack aircraft fell off the side of the aircraft carrier [USS _Ticonderoga_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Ticonderoga_(CV-14) "USS Ticonderoga (CV-14)"). The jet, pilot and weapon were not recovered.

### 1966: U.S. strategic bomber crash in Spain

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: 1966: U.S. strategic bomber crash in Spain")]

A B-52G bomber and [KC-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KC-135 "KC-135") tanker crashed over the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea"). The bomber was carrying nuclear weapons at the time. While the bombs did not detonate, they did [contaminate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radioactive_contamination "Radioactive contamination") the area with radioactive material.

### 1966: French false alarm from weather (likely)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: 1966: French false alarm from weather (likely)")]

In the early days of the French [Strategic Air Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Forces_Command "Strategic Air Forces Command"), electrical transmissions were disrupted due to a thunderstorm, causing a wartime takeoff order to be displayed. The [French Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Air_and_Space_Force "French Air and Space Force") launched a [Mirage IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dassault_Mirage_IV "Dassault Mirage IV") with an [AN-11 atomic bomb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AN-11_bomb "AN-11 bomb"). The crew was called back by radio, but did not respond, as required by procedure. When they reached their refueling zone, they were unable to find the supply plane, forcing them to abort their mission, turn back, and land.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-96)

### 1967: U.S. false alarm from weather

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: 1967: U.S. false alarm from weather")]

A powerful [solar flare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_flare "Solar flare") accompanied by a [coronal mass ejection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronal_mass_ejection "Coronal mass ejection") interfered with multiple [NORAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NORAD "NORAD") radars over the [Northern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Hemisphere "Northern Hemisphere"). These radars included three [Ballistic Missile Early Warning Systems (BMEWS)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistic_Missile_Early_Warning_System "Ballistic Missile Early Warning System") that had been recently upgraded, and only resumed operation eight days prior to the flare.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-97) This interference was initially interpreted as [intentional jamming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar_jamming_and_deception "Radar jamming and deception") of the radars by the Soviets, and thus an act of war. A nuclear bomber [counterstrike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterattack "Counterattack") was nearly launched by the United States.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-98) The Strategic Air Command had prepared to launch fighters before NORAD alerted them of the solar flare.

### 1968: U.S. strategic bomber crash in Greenland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=38 "Edit section: 1968: U.S. strategic bomber crash in Greenland")]

A fire broke out on a nuclear-armed B-52 bomber just off Greenland, and the plane crashed into the sea without causing a detonation.

### 1979: U.S. false alarm from computer training scenario

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=39 "Edit section: 1979: U.S. false alarm from computer training scenario")]

Computer errors at the [NORAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NORAD "NORAD") headquarters in [Peterson Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peterson_Air_Force_Base "Peterson Air Force Base"), the [Strategic Air Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_Air_Command "Strategic Air Command") command post in [Offutt Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offutt_Air_Force_Base "Offutt Air Force Base"), the [National Military Command Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Military_Command_Center "National Military Command Center") in the [Pentagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon "The Pentagon"), and the [Alternate National Military Command Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternate_National_Military_Command_Center "Alternate National Military Command Center") in the [Raven Rock Mountain Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raven_Rock_Mountain_Complex "Raven Rock Mountain Complex") led to alarm and full preparation for a nonexistent large-scale Soviet attack.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-nuclear_files_20-5)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-UCS_close_calls-87) NORAD notified [National Security Advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Advisor_(United_States) "National Security Advisor (United States)")[Zbigniew Brzezinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zbigniew_Brzezinski "Zbigniew Brzezinski") that the Soviet Union had launched 250 [ballistic missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistic_missile "Ballistic missile") with a trajectory for the United States, stating that a decision to retaliate would need to be made by the president within three to seven minutes. NORAD computers then placed the number of incoming missiles at 2,200.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-The_3_A.M._Phone_Call-99) Strategic Air Command was notified, and nuclear bombers prepared for takeoff. Within six to seven minutes of the initial response, [PAVE PAWS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PAVE_PAWS "PAVE PAWS") satellite and radar systems were able to confirm that the attack was a false alarm.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-nuclear_files_20-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-:0-6)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-100)

[Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") quickly learned of the incident because Senator [Charles H. Percy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_H._Percy "Charles H. Percy") was present at the NORAD headquarters during the panic. A [General Accounting Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Accountability_Office "Government Accountability Office") investigation found that a training scenario was inadvertently loaded into an operational computer in the [Cheyenne Mountain Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheyenne_Mountain_Complex "Cheyenne Mountain Complex").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-nuclear_files_20-5) Commenting on the incident, [U.S. State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State "United States Department of State") adviser [Marshall Shulman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_D._Shulman "Marshall D. Shulman") stated that "false alerts of this kind are not a rare occurrence. There is a complacency about handling them that disturbs me."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-The_3_A.M._Phone_Call-99)[Soviet General Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union "General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union")[Leonid Brezhnev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonid_Brezhnev "Leonid Brezhnev") composed a letter to U.S. President [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") that the false alarm was "fraught with a tremendous danger" and "I think you will agree with me that there should be no errors in such matters."[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-:1-101) In the months following the incident, there were three more false alarms at NORAD, two of them caused by faulty [computer chips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_circuit "Integrated circuit").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-UCS_close_calls-87) One of them forced the [National Emergency Airborne Command Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Emergency_Air-Borne_Command_Post "National Emergency Air-Borne Command Post") to taxi into position at [Andrews Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrews_Air_Force_Base "Andrews Air Force Base").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-:1-101)

### 1980: U.S. false alarm from Soviet missile exercise

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=40 "Edit section: 1980: U.S. false alarm from Soviet missile exercise")]

A Soviet submarine near the [Kuril Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuril_Islands "Kuril Islands") launched four missiles as part of a [training exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_exercise "Military exercise"). American early warning sensors determined one of the four to be aimed towards the United States. In response, the United States convened officials for a threat assessment conference, at which point it was determined to not be a threat and the situation was resolved.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-UCS_close_calls-87)

### 1980: Explosion at U.S. missile silo

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=41 "Edit section: 1980: Explosion at U.S. missile silo")]

An explosion in [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas") ripped the doors off a silo and launched part of a nuclear missile out of the structure. The warhead landed 30m away, but safety features prevented either a detonation or release of radioactive material. The incident caused one death and 21 injuries, and sparked a congressional inquiry.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-102)

### 1983: Soviet false alarm from weather (likely)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=42 "Edit section: 1983: Soviet false alarm from weather (likely)")]

Several weeks after the downing of [Korean Air Lines Flight 007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Air_Lines_Flight_007 "Korean Air Lines Flight 007") over Soviet airspace, a satellite early warning system near Moscow reported the launch of one American [Minuteman ICBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGM-30_Minuteman "LGM-30 Minuteman"). Soon after, it reported that five missiles had been launched. Convinced that a real American offensive would involve many more missiles, Lieutenant Colonel [Stanislav Petrov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanislav_Petrov "Stanislav Petrov") of the [Air Defense Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Air_Defence_Forces "Soviet Air Defence Forces") refused to acknowledge the threat as legitimate and continued to convince his superiors that it was a false alarm until this could be confirmed by ground [radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radar "Radar").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-:0-6)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-wash-103)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-Baltimore_Sun-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-PetrovBBC-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-PetrovAP-106)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-PetrovNPR-107)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-PetrovSmithsonian-108)[_[excessive citations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing\_sources#Bundling\_citations "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_]

### 1991: Tornado at U.S. strategic bomber airbase

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=43 "Edit section: 1991: Tornado at U.S. strategic bomber airbase")]

On April 26, 1991, a large tornado touched down southwest of the city of [Wichita, Kansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wichita,_Kansas "Wichita, Kansas"), heading towards the city of [Andover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andover,_Kansas "Andover, Kansas"). As the tornado approached Andover, it struck the [McConnell Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McConnell_Air_Force_Base "McConnell Air Force Base"), where it narrowly missed ten lined up [Rockwell B-1 Lancers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_B-1_Lancer "Rockwell B-1 Lancer"), two of them armed with nuclear warheads.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-109)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-111)

### 1995: Russian false alarm from Norwegian research rocket

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=44 "Edit section: 1995: Russian false alarm from Norwegian research rocket")]

[Russian President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Russia "President of Russia")[Boris Yeltsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Yeltsin "Boris Yeltsin") became the first world leader to activate the [Russian nuclear briefcase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheget "Cheget") after Russian radar systems detected the launch of what was later determined to be a Norwegian [Black Brant XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Brant_XII "Black Brant XII") research rocket being used to study the [northern lights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurora "Aurora").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-112) Russian [ballistic missile submarines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballistic_missile_submarine "Ballistic missile submarine") were put on alert in preparation for a possible retaliatory strike.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-113) When it became clear the rocket did not pose a threat to Russia and was not part of a larger attack, the alarm was cancelled. Russia was, in fact, one of a number of countries earlier informed of the launch; however, the information had not reached the Russian radar operators.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-UCS_close_calls-87)

### 2007: Improper transport of U.S. nuclear weapons

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nuclear_close_calls&action=edit&section=45 "Edit section: 2007: Improper transport of U.S. nuclear weapons")]

On 29 August 2007, six nuclear-armed [AGM-129 ACM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AGM-129_ACM "AGM-129 ACM")[cruise missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cruise_missile "Cruise missile") were mistakenly loaded onto a [United States Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") (USAF) [B-52H](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B-52H "B-52H")[heavy bomber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_bomber "Heavy bomber") at [Minot Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minot_Air_Force_Base "Minot Air Force Base") in [North Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Dakota "North Dakota") and transported to [Barksdale Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barksdale_Air_Force_Base "Barksdale Air Force Base") in [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"). The nuclear warheads in the missiles were supposed to have been removed before the missiles were taken from their storage bunker. The missiles with the nuclear warheads were not reported missing and remained mounted to the aircraft at both Minot and Barksdale for 36 hours. During this period, the warheads were not protected by the various mandatory security precautions for nuclear weapons, and the government was not aware of their location. The incident was the [first of its kind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bent_Spear "Bent Spear") in 40 years in the United States and was later described by the media as "one of the worst breaches in U.S. nuclear weapons security in decades".[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_nuclear_close_calls#cite_note-114)
